questions.prompt: MFA was enforced and worked correctly. Why did it not prevent the compromise?
options: The attacker bypassed MFA with a stolen token
The attack never needed a password -- the user authenticated properly and then authorized a malicious application, which MFA is not a control against
MFA was only enforced for administrators
The attacker registered their own MFA method first
questions.explanation: An illicit consent grant obtains access through legitimate authorization rather than credential theft, so authentication controls are simply not in the path.

questions.prompt: Why did the immediate password reset fail to terminate access?
options: The reset did not replicate to the cloud
The refresh token granted by offline_access was unaffected, and the OAuth grant had never depended on the password at all
The attacker had already changed the password back
The reset required a second application to take effect
questions.explanation: Audit logs showed the attacker still reading mail forty minutes after the reset -- access ended only once the grant, service principal, and refresh tokens were all addressed.

questions.prompt: Why did the fraudulent wire instruction message pass SPF, DKIM, and DMARC?
options: The attacker forged the DKIM signature
It was genuinely sent from the real mailbox on the real tenant -- the authentication was correct because the message actually was from Contoso
The client's mail server had authentication disabled
The attacker used a lookalike domain for that message
questions.explanation: Email authentication verifies the sending domain, not the sender's intent. A compromised legitimate mailbox passes every check by design.

questions.prompt: Which single control would have removed the entire attack surface?
options: Restricting user consent to verified publishers and low-impact permissions
questions.explanation: A tenant-level consent restriction prevents ordinary users granting the permissions the attack depends on, eliminating the initial step entirely.
